Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Labour will no doubt have received a report in this regard, but I should like to ask him now what is the present position regarding 23033-375
the strike, which more and more is bringing about disastrous stagnation.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. R. Nicholson (Minister of Labour):
subtopic: QUEBEC LONGSHOREMEN'S STRIKE-REQUEST FOR REPORT ON NEGOTIATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sure that it will not be news to most members of the house that the mediator, Judge Lippe, had a difficult day yesterday. Nevertheless I think he performed a useful service in keeping the parties together working toward a settlement.
Late yesterday Judge Lippe announced his recommendation to both sides regarding a commission of inquiry which he felt should be set up. That suggestion was to be given consideration overnight. I may say that following the meeting with the mediator the longshoremen suggested that a meeting with the stevedoring companies should be held. A telegram was sent to the Prime Minister last night on this subject, and at the request of the Prime Minister I replied to it early this morning. In view of the publicity that has been given to this matter it might be wise, with the permission of the house, to read into the record the telegram of reply.
It is addressed to Mr. Paul Asselin and Mr. Gerard Tremblay, one of whom is the president of the largest longshoremen's union in Quebec, the Montreal union, and the other is international vice president. The telegram reads as follows:
The Prime Minister has received your telegram of June 2 and has asked me to reply. I would first say that any suggestion for the early settlement of the strike of longshoremen at St. Lawrence ports is greatly welcomed here. With respect to your suggestion that the shipping federation be displaced as the bargaining representative for the employers they represent you will recall that in the various certificates granted to your organization by the wartime and Canada labour relations boards the shipping federation was named as the representative of the various employers affected. It is not in my power to displace either the federation or your organization as the representative agencies of the employers or the employees affected by the dispute. I would hope that both parties resume collective bargaining to restore the good relations that existed for many years in the past.
I would supplement this information by saying that the wire has gone out and my deputy minister is still in Montreal with Judge Lippe, working on this matter as one of greatest urgency.

June 3, 1966
Inquiries of the Ministry

subtopic: QUEBEC LONGSHOREMEN'S STRIKE-REQUEST FOR REPORT ON NEGOTIATIONS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, could the minister also read into the record the telegram that was sent to the Prime Minister, so we will have the full record; and will he say whether the displacement of the shipping federation is a condition precedent, in so far as the stevedores' organization is concerned, to a settlement?

speechtext:
I have no objection, if the house is willing, to reading into the record the wire that was received by the Prime Minister. I might say that there are some points in it that are open to argument. Perhaps that is not surprising in disputes of this nature; you get them from one side or the other. The wire to the Prime Minister reads as follows:
Must regretfully advise you that the International Longshoremen's Association now finds it evident that it cannot settle its dispute with the customers of its employers. The employers of the longshoremen at Montreal, Quebec and Three Rivers are the undernoted stevedoring companies duly incorporated in Canada and owned and operated by Canadians. The International Longshoremen's Association have by circumstance been placed in the position of dealing with the Shipping Federation of Canada the members of which are not our employers but are in fact foreign steamship companies for the most part located in Great Britain.
That is not strictly accurate, because there are some Canadian companies in this federation as well.

No, I interjected that.

It is obvious that the capricious attitude of the Shipping Federation of Canada and our members are convinced that if the shipping federation remains in command of the negotiations relevant to a proposed collective agreement between our organization its members and various Canadian stevedore companies the said collective agreement will be blocked by its present impasse until such times as the dispute in Great Britain with the British sailors is settled.
Respectfully petition the labour minister to direct that the negotiations be conducted between the International Longshoremen's Association and the employers of its members, which are namely the following Canadian stevedore companies: Brown and Ryan, Eastern Canada, Wolfe Stevedores, Cullen Stevedores, Montreal, and Saint John Stevedores, etc. etc. It is our earnest belief that action by the hon. minister upon this justified petition will result in a settlement of this dispute within a relatively short period.

Gerard Tremblay

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to direct a question to the right hon. Prime Minister. Would he inform the house whether the government has received any protest from the Soviet union against alleged anti-Soviet propaganda in Canada, and what reply the government has given or is preparing to counter such allegations.
Inquiries of the Ministry

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. B. Pearson (Prime Minister):
subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: RUSSIA-REPORTED COMPLAINT AGAINST CAMPAIGN IN CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the matter to which my hon. friend refers was the subject of representations made to a member of our embassy in Moscow at the Soviet foreign ministry on June 1. The Soviet embassy here and Soviet officials in Moscow have recently made known to us informally their concern at what they refer to as an anti-Soviet campaign in the Canadian press, citing what they consider to be evidence from press reports to support their concern. We have explained that such reporting is a normal function of the press in a free society, and that what the press prints is in no way controlled by the government. We have assured them that it remains a sincere desire of the Canadian government to encourage the development of mutually beneficial relations between Canada and the Soviet union.
In this connection I think I can say with your concurrence, Mr. Speaker, that not only the government but all of us in this house are greatly looking forward to the forthcoming visit to Canada of Soviet parliamentarians led by the first deputy premier, Dimitri Polyansky, and to their subsequent tour of the grain growing areas in western Canada. I am not aware, Mr. Speaker, of any so-called provocations directed against the Soviet embassy nor of any activity which might impede its normal functions.

[DOT] (11:50 a.m.)

It is not often that I agree with the hon. member for York South, but on this occasion I do agree with him. Because there has been so much dissatisfaction expressed by hon. members about the minister's designated areas policy, if he will not consider discontinuing the policy, the suggestion that item 1 of the estimates stand and
June 3, 1966

the rest of the estimates be proceeded with might be considered. The minister has made an accusation that possibly there is filibustering on the part of the opposition. This is not filibustering. It has been pointed out previously that it is the duty of the opposition to criticize bad legislation. After hearing all the speeches about designated areas surely the minister must realize that this is a bad policy, but he has given no indication whatsoever that he will waver or bend just a little bit. He has not said he will take the legislation and reconsider it. He has not set a limit on how long he is going to carry out this policy.
This policy is bad for a number of reasons. It is bad for industry. It is not helping industry even though the minister tries to indicate that it is. Surely the minister is not so blind that he cannot bend just a little bit and give some consideration to the speeches made not only by the opposition but by his own backbenchers. In fact I heard only one speech from the government side supporting the minister's policy, and I heard many speakers on the government backbenches saying it is a bad policy. Surely those people have some influence on the minister, and I suggest we stand this item until we dispose of the rest of the estimates.

May I ask the minister a

speakerposition: Minister of Industry; Minister of Defence Production
speechtext:
Just one moment, please. There seems to be some misconception as to how the program operates. There seem to be differences of view as to whether it should be extended, and as to the areas in which it should be extended. Mr. Chairman, in view of what the minister has just said I am just wondering how far the hon. member for Timiskaming wants this designated area program expanded. If the minister thinks we are going to get down on our hands and knees and crawl to him, asking him to include each of our own areas and in that way get rid of the opposition, he has another think coming. I would also say it should be extended, but I would go further than my own community. I would say it should be extended to the whole of Canada. Then it would not be discriminatory as it is at present.
The minister says I am a minority of one. Surely the minister, if he did not listen, must have looked over the speeches of members on this side of the house. There were very few

who complimented him on this type of policy. Certainly those who benefit from the legislation are in favour of it, but I say that in designating these areas the minister has not used the same criteria in all cases. I know certain representations have been made to the minister. I know he has changed his mind and designated certain areas, but I refuse to beg him to designate my area. That is what the minister wants.
I say that if the minister were not so arrogant and did not have the mind of a civil servant he would realize what is happening in this chamber today, namely that the people are speaking. Canada dislikes this policy that has been put forward by the minister. There are many areas in Canada that do not like it. Because pressure has been put on the minister by certain industrial urban centres he says they like it, but there are many rural areas in this country, and the people in them also have to make a living. Because of this policy, as has been pointed out to the minister on many previous occasions, the standard of living in those areas is dropping.
Family income is going down because of this very policy for which the minister is seeking support. This is what we are fighting against. It is to this that we want him to give consideration. I say stop this discrimination or extend the policy to cover all of Canada. I do not care which the minister does.

Mr. Chairman, I almost rose on a point of order on something said by the minister a few minutes ago. He said it was the opinion held by a minority of one in this chamber that the present policy pursued by his department regarding these designated areas was a poor policy. I would like to refute that.

speakerposition: Minister of Industry; Minister of Defence Production
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, perhaps I was misunderstood. I did not say that the policy was universally approved either by members of the committee or by Canada. What I did say is that a very small minority would like to see the policy abandoned, and the hon. member for Swift Current-Maple Creek wanted it completely withdrawn. Now, there are a number of people who would like to see it changed-
How does it help industry?

speakerposition: Minister of Industry; Minister of Defence Production
speechtext:
-and I receive continuous representations regarding change. One further means of exploring suggested changes is consideration of the program by a committee. I

am delighted to agree to this, and have already agreed to it.
[DOT] (12:00 noon)
I am not saying the policy is perfect; I know it is not. The hon. member for Swift Current-Maple Creek suggested that it is a discriminatory policy and that one should remove the discrimination by extending it to all Canada. This is an incentive program. By definition an incentive program must be discriminatory. It must appeal to a limited segment and not to universality if it is going to be an incentive. The object of the program is to provide assistance in the way of incentives to those areas suffering from high chronic unemployment, and the whole of Canada does not suffer from high chronic unemployment. If, as the hon. member for Swift Current-Maple Creek suggests, the criteria are not being applied properly, I would be delighted to learn where they are not being applied properly. I think they are. Perhaps in the committee examples of where they are not being applied properly can be adduced and a detailed answer given. I myself believe they are being properly and objectively applied.
It does not rest with the hon. member for Swift Current-Maple Creek, as he puts it, to come on his knees to me to get his area designated. I do not do the designation. As I pointed out last night the designation is quite automatic; it is determined by local events. When the chronic unemployment in a national employment service area, as measured by national employment registrations or by the average non-farm family income, rises in the case of registrations above a certain level or goes below, in terms of average family income, a certain point, that area qualifies itself quite independently of any views I may have on the subject. As I say, the qualification for designation is determined by local events and not at the discretion of the minister or the department. There is no discretion. When the local situation falls within the framework laid down by the act and the order in council designation takes place, and not at the discretion of either myself or the officials. So not only can the member spare his knees so far as I am concerned, but I can say further that it would not do him any good if he did come to me on bended knees. It would be a wasted pilgrimage.

Mr. Chairman, I thank the minister for his attempt to explain his version of the feelings on this side of the house but his explanation is unsatisfactory so far as
June 3, 1966

I am concerned, so far as my riding is concerned and so far as a vast area of southern Ontario with which I am familiar is concerned. I support the hon. member for Swift Current-Maple Creek in his contention that this legislation is discriminatory and is bad for Canada as a whole. It even reflects on the motives of this government, when one goes back and analyses the primary reason for bringing in such legislation. On May 17 I protested against it because representations had been made to me from both the counties I represent, the county of Prince Edward and the county of Lennox, where the people are completely frustrated. They cannot get any new industry because of the attractive propositions put forward by the government to induce the location of industry in neighbouring areas which are designated.
My area, like that of the hon. member for Swift Current-Maple Creek, is not designated. May I also say to the minister that I do not believe the hon. member for Swift Current-Maple Creek is coming on his knees to anyone in an effort to have his area designated. I think that applies to my people too. We do not come on our knees imploring assistance from the minister, who has designated other areas near us, but we do ask for fair play all across the board regarding our efforts to obtain industry. Despite our qualifications for assimilation of new industry, a month ago the county of Prince Edward was turned down by an industry because the people who represented the industry said they could not accept our offers in the face of the attractive offers made by the Department of Industry with regard to designated areas. They have gone to a designated area.
The minister has said that his policy in respect of designated areas is successful. That may be so, but it has been disastrous to non-designated areas. He is carrying out this policy at the expense of the rest of Canada and the taxpayers thereof. In the non-desig-nated areas, which the government of course must have decided were industrially healthy, the people there also pay the taxes to help finance the designated area plan and they certainly are not in favour of it. It is unfair, discriminatory and very frustrating to hundreds of municipal councils and chambers of commerce. Hundreds of municipalities and towns all across Canada place a levy on their taxpayers to finance programs designed to attract industry. The designated area program is stultifying all their efforts and nullifying whatever they hope to accomplish in 23033-3761

the current year because of the better offers made and the larger grants paid by the government to prospective industry if it will settle in an area where the government wants it to settle.
There is nothing fair about this plan. The whole of Canada is watching it. I caution the minister. A few minutes ago he said that if it did not work he would make changes. I admonish the minister and his department right now to forget about this idea and be fair to the whole country.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I certainly am not going to take up too much of the time of the committee. I know that is a popular saying at this stage of estimates. I have, however, been provoked into speaking this afternoon because of several statements made and the attitude adopted. I cannot say I agree entirely with the hon. member for Swift Current-Maple Creek but that is not unusual. I might say I am saying that in a personal vein. I should like to say also that I think that some of the things he said are completely true, particularly in regard to attitude.
I wish to make one thing very clear. In the areas which have been designated and have had the benefit of this assistance, I think the policy has certainly been successful. The minister knows the representations I made to him earlier. I was amazed at some of the answers he gave me last evening to pointed questions, but I should like to make an observation in respect of his approach. I recall very well an occasion when I accompanied a large delegation from several different constituencies. At that time the minister unfortunately was not present. As a matter of fact, the reception I received on that occasion from the present Minister of Finance was warm, sensible and sympathetic. The results of the meeting were nil, not because of the attitude of the Minister of Finance but because of the general attitude taken by the Minister of Industry.
[DOT] (12:10 p.m.)
Let me make a brief comparison as to what has happened in various areas. The minister tells me that on a statistical basis he does not, strictly speaking, make any decisions at all as to designation but that various areas are designated because of their particular circumstances. Let us consider the counties of Grey and Bruce and other associated counties in that part of the Georgian bay area. I hold no feeling whatsoever against the people who

June 3, 1966
Supply-Industry
have the advantage of designation. The results of designation have been wonderful and the advantages enjoyed by the people there have been tremendous. Let us consider the town of Kincardine, which is not in my constituency, and the towns of Southampton and Port Elgin. The latter two fall within a designated area whereas Kincardine does not. There is no justification for this fact at all.
Let us compare the situations of the town of Walkerton and the city of Midland. There is no comparison at all and the designation of Midland is ridiculous. The city of Midland enjoys the highest rate of employment that any community could wish but the advantages of designation are given to it and not to Walkerton. Let us compare the situations of the towns of Chesley and Meaford. There is no comparison there, yet one has the advantages of designation. Let us compare the towns of Port Elgin and Kincardine, the towns of Walkerton and Owen Sound, or let us compare them with Midland again. There is no comparison at all. Yet some have the advantages of designation and others do not.
The minister tells me that all these places qualify because of their own circumstances, but that statement is utterly ridiculous. I assure the minister that I am not making these remarks to antagonize him. At one time it was said to me: Do you want to accept the responsibility of removing the designation from the Georgian bay area? I said no and I say no again this afternoon. However, I certainly would be willing to accept the responsibility for designating the balance of the Georgian bay economic region as established by the province of Ontario.
This sort of designation nonsense has got to stop. If we are going to consider economic areas as such let us consider them that way. What is the minister trying to do, play politics with these designations? I do not think he is because he has not had any success in that area as shown by the lack of elected members in the government party. These designations should be made on a moral and sensible basis. I was informed, I think by an official of the minister's department, that all the economic factors were taken into consideration in designating an area. I asked what was meant by that and I was told that the factors taken into consideration include income from welfare and that sort of thing. Goodness me, if we are going to consider pensions and old age assistance in respect of the criteria we are not being honest about the situation. Certainly that is

not an honest or fair approach. In the particular areas to which I have referred the young people do not remain there because there is no incentive. If we are given the incentive to attract industry to our area we will be able to keep our young people working there, but the minister is not prepared to give us that incentive.
This government has taken a dictatorial attitude in that we are going to have universality in respect of everything. We have been forced to pay into the Canada Pension Plan and we will be forced to pay into medicare. Yet the minister is forcing the people who should enjoy the benefits of designation right out of the areas where they now live. This is a totally wrong attitude on the part of the minister and his department and I believe a revision of thinking should take place.
I am sure everyone recalls the discussion that took place here last week regarding the proposed increases in tolls on St. Lawrence seaway and the Welland canal. This is another factor that will deprive us of a certain element of growth. If we are going to create something that will be of benefit to people, let us not put roadblocks in the way.
Not long ago I asked the Minister of Agriculture where on earth all the pork came from that was imported into this country. We appealed to the government to assist this section of the agricultural industry, but it allowed approximately 2,500,000 pounds of pork to be imported by a processer for the express purpose of depressing an industry which exists in the area. In spite of that fact the minister and his department will not give us what they could give us by way of designation. The minister must change his attitude in this regard.
Let me return to my original statement. I brought a group of people to Ottawa to meet with the minister and officials of his department. In my view the delegation took a very moral and sensible attitude toward the situation. I am sure the minister realizes that the people in our area have the ability to attract industry but, for goodness sake, give them every advantage they can get in their attempt to create a large area of development in western Ontario. All I am asking the minister to do is to revise his policy and for designation purposes to use the boundaries of the economic divisions set up by the department of development and economics of the province of Ontario. That department has attempted to do a good job but it is being discriminated against by the policy of the
June 3, 1966

minister and his department. If we are going to have reasonable and sensible area development and if we are going to spend the kind of money involved, for goodness sake let the minister and the department adopt a fair and moral attitude.
I was ridiculed a few weeks ago when I argued against the redistribution of my area as a result of which my constituency will disappear. However, the government is according me one honour in that I will be the last member to represent the riding of Grey-Bruce with the distinction that the members for that constituency have brought to the House of Commons over the years. However, the people I have the honour of representing now will be disregarded even more after redistribution because of being lost in the big shuffle. There is enough disregard now for this part of the province of Ontario, and these are the people for whom I have great concern. We have the ability to attract industrial organizations to our area and we have proven that in the past, but you are not going to accomplish decentralization in this area by compounding the problem through discriminatory action.
I do not intend to come to the minister on bended knee requesting that this area be given the advantages of the designation program. As a matter of fact, after my last experience I would not even waste the time required to make another request. I do ask the minister to take a further look at this situation and act in a fair and moral way in determining government policy and its application so that the area can be given the advantages that are being afforded to other areas in this country.

Mr. Chairman, to change the pace I should like to obtain some information from the Minister of Industry. Will the minister indicate the number of areas that have been added to the list of designated areas under this plan? I have talked with the minister about this subject and I think he knows what I have in mind. As an example, the Grand Forks area was added to the Okanagan designated area. I am wondering how many similar areas in Canada have been added to other designated areas. How many contiguous areas have been added to existing designated areas?

speakerposition: Minister of Industry; Minister of Defence Production
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I am not sure I can answer that question or that I really understand it. The problem of designation involves the identification of areas of high
Supply-Industry
chronic unemployment. In order to identify them and provide assistance one must have information relating to employment. There has been a system in existence for a number of years under the national employment service of gathering and collating statistical information in relation to national employment service areas. This information is gathered and related to an area as a whole rather than to segments or individual parts. In our search for some means of identifying large areas in Canada suffering from high chronic unemployment the only measuring stick available was that provided by N.E.S. statistics. For that reason the N.E.S. areas provide the framework for designation, and when in a given N.E.S. area the pattern of unemployment is above a certain figure the area becomes designated. When the unemployment pattern falls below a certain figure the area is de-designated.
[DOT] (12:20 p.m.)
The process of creating designated areas in hitherto undesignated areas and designating those areas whose level of employment has fallen has been taking place ever since the beginning of the program. I am not sure whether the hon. member is asking me for a list of areas which were designated at the beginning of the program and have been de-designated. If this is so, I would be glad to give him this information. It is all contained in the original order in council which was tabled and in the subsequent order in council which was also tabled.

Mr. Chairman, my question did not refer to how many areas have been brought into the program and designated, and I am quite aware of the use of N.E.S. figures. I refer to the adding of an area which would normally be considered as having chronic unemployment to an already designated area. I believe that the town of Blairmore, Alberta, has been added quite recently to an area in British Columbia. This is my understanding after talking to the Liberal member from that area. I am wondering-

speakerposition: Minister of Industry; Minister of Defence Production
speechtext:
Let me interrupt for a moment, Mr. Chairman, to say that the Blairmore N.E.S. area, including the town of Blairmore, has been designated from the outset of the program. It was amongst the first areas to be designated and has continued to be designated ever since. There has been no change in respect of the town of Blairmore.

June 3, 1966
Supply-Industry
Then might I ask the minister whether any area has been added to a designated area, the area added being of such a nature that in itself it would not qualify under the N.E.S. formula?

speakerposition: Minister of Industry; Minister of Defence Production
speechtext:
In respect of areas which in themselves might not qualify but have been designated, this applies to some census divisions and some counties contiguous to and touching on N.E.S. areas which have been designated. I think we discussed yesterday census divisions 12 and 13 in northern Alberta. I am not sure whether this is what the hon. gentleman refers to or whether he is looking at the situation in British Columbia. It may be that he is thinking of changes in the boundaries of the N.E.S. areas themselves. This is quite unrelated to designated areas.
The National Employment Service has over the years changed the pattern, shape and size of individual National Employment Service areas. This is done continually. As the economy of an N.E.S. area changes and development takes place in that general area of the country, perhaps the boundaries, as in the case of boundaries of political constituencies, are no longer appropriate. Previously the Department of Labour had responsibility in this regard but now it is the Department of Citizenship and Immigration and it is continually looking at the size, shape and structure of the National Employment Service areas for national employment purposes. They periodically redraw these boundaries in the same way that the boundaries of political constituencies are periodically redrawn.
This happened in relation to the Vernon N.E.S. area. The boundaries that existed some three years ago did not seem to correspond any more to the economic facts of that region so the boundaries were changed. This is how Salmon Arm came to be included. The assumption is that it has been put into a designated area. In fact, what happened was that Salmon Arm was put into the Vernon N.E.S. area. The question now is whether Sicamous should also be included in that N.E.S. area. This has nothing to do with designation at all. I hope I have made myself clear.
An interdepartmental committee is now studying the N.E.S. areas all the way across the country to see how appropriate they are to current circumstances in the light of representations that have been made by a number of people, including the hon. member for Grey-Bruce. That hon. member's basic

unhappiness arises out of the fact that he does not like the way in which the National Employment Service has drawn the boundaries of the two N.E.S. areas in his constituency. Both these areas are in his county. The result is that part of his constituency is in an N.E.S. area which has been designated and part is in an N.E.S. area which has not been designated. The hon. member for Grey-Bruce would like the whole of his constituency to be designated. This is understandable.
There is no doubt that economic conditions close to and on either side of an N.E.S. line would be roughly similar. This is in the nature of things. Whether the dividing line should be a little north, south, east or west is something that is now being examined not only with regard to the Pembina area but for all N.E.S. areas in Canada.

I should like to clear up one point, Mr. Chairman, because I think it is fairly important. The minister has said that in the efflux of time there have been changes in economic conditions and other circumstances which have resulted in the N.E.S. boundaries being changed. I wish to pinpoint one thing. Has any area been added to a designated area, at the request of the people in the area added, with no redrawing of the N.E.S. boundaries? This is the specific question. I am relating it precisely to the Grand Forks area, about which the minister knows, and the Okanagan Boundary designated area. Grand Forks is not designated; the Okanagan Valley is. Has any similar area been added to an already designated area other than with respect to N.E.S. boundary changes?

speakerposition: Minister of Industry; Minister of Defence Production
speechtext: I can say no quite categorically, Mr. Chairman, and I hope this will never occur. speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Will the hon. member permit a question? Does he not think that $20 million spent on technical and vocational schools in Newfoundland was of some good to that province?

I said you did some good and that was one of the good things, possibly one of the best, but it was one of the very few things. Under this program we will have 15 or 16 brand new industries, and some 36 million brand new dollars which we know will be used to provide a projected 1,000 brand new jobs. This is the kind of legislation we want. May I therefore congratulate the minister once again on his imaginative and liberal program.

Mr. Chairman, I was very surprised to hear the member for St. John's East contribute to this debate. He reminds me of the story of the father who had two sons. He rewarded one and punished the other. It is like the fellow who receives something and then thanks you for it. I think the hon. member has taken a very narrow view in regard to the regions which are being discriminated against. This is the point we are trying to discuss. I heard the minister say in answer to the member for Okanagan Boundary that industry was induced to locate in certain areas for the sake of temporary relief of the unemployment problem. I say to the minister that this is a very expensive way of dealing with that problem.
As I said before, it is not the Department of Industry which should be dealing with unemployment but the Department of Labour because this program was not primarily designed to help the unemployed. As Shakespeare said, "What's in a name? That which we call a rose by any other name would smell as sweet." The minister has been trying to tell us that this program assists industry. This
Supply-Industry
is not so; it is purely a labour program and should be left with the Department of Labour.
It is certainly true that these grants assist industry but, as I said before, they represent a short-range view of the problem of industry. You are forcing industries to locate in areas in which they do not wish to locate because of certain special factors and by offering incentives or bribes which you give to them under the guise of grants and writeoffs. It is only for this reason that they in fact locate their plants where you wish them to. However, if they took a long-term view of the economy of Canada, our foreign trade and everything else, they would choose other locations than the minister is forcing them to choose at the present time.
I agree with the minister that this program is not all bad; there must be some good in it. For instance, we have the example given by the hon. member for St. John's East of the $36 million received by Newfoundland which it would not have received if the program had not been put into effect. Nevertheless this was done at the expense of the non-designat-ed areas. Is that fair? I think it is discrimination. You are playing one region against the other. This is not fair from the point of view of the decentralization of industry and it is not fair with regard to the continuing problems that these regions will have. Above all, it is not fair to industry because, as I said earlier, you are creating problems which will be very difficult to overcome in the future when the incentive program is completed.
I also say to the minister that this is a very expensive way of dealing with the problem of unemployment. These are much better ways.

Apparently the minister
does not understand what we are trying to get across. I was going to tell him why this program is dangerous to the future of Canada, to its economy and its foreign trade. This is what we are trying to stop. If the minister wishes me to go into detail, I will certainly do so. I will also acquiesce to such a wish from the hon. member for St. John's East.
I simply wish to say at this time that this is a very expensive way of providing temporary relief for the unemployment situation in Canada. It is not an answer to that problem. We ask the minister to reconsider the program and change it to make it non-discriminatory.
Yesterday I listed many of the underprivileged areas. The minister is being unfair to many regions in Canada. I wish to draw the minister's attention to this fact. He said something about waiting for me to make a pilgrimage to his door. I say to the minister, don't hold your breath too long because you will never see the day when I will come to your door on my knees.

Mr. Chairman, if anything has come out of this debate it has been the general dissatisfaction with the area incentive program. In his opening remarks yesterday the minister chose to interpret the fact that there is so much opposition to this program as an indication of its success. He was pleased with the fact that people were putting forward different points of view. He interpreted this as a positive approach to this program. I would suggest to the minister that the contrary is probably true.
All of us surely recognize, in fairness to the minister, how difficult it is to implement such a program and how difficult it is to satisfy people with an area designated program which, as he points out himself, must of necessity be discriminatory in order to be effective. We realize he has to face a difficult problem.
I also think very few of us would quarrel with the idea of an area development program. We know there are disadvantaged regions in Canada, that many of these areas face difficult problems and that we have a responsibility to do whatever we can in their behalf. No one is arguing about this general principle. What we are quarrelling about, and the issue which we are now raising, concerns the particular method which the minister has chosen to implement area designation by using certain types of criteria.
[The Chairman.]
He has also explored other criteria, I am sure. As has been pointed out by some other speakers in this debate, to limit the criteria to the problem of unemployment is taking a short-range view of the situation. This is not an adequate concept of the area development program. I presume this is a formula which the minister has devised in order to ensure that no one will point a finger at him and say he is being arbitrary. It is a very rigid formula based on unemployment, income and other contingencies, and in this way he thinks he is being fair in the administration of the program. According to this formula, an area is eligible for the program if it falls within these criteria. This is really a lazy man's program and I do not believe the minister is a lazy man. He is certainly a most active man. He has implemented new programs and he has stuck his neck out on many occasions. However, this particular program is a lazy man's program. He is throwing things into the hopper and hoping they will work out.
* (12:40 p.m.)
In other words, the program requires a minimum amount of administration, a minimum amount of decision-making in order to make it work. Either an area fits or it does not fit. Everything is being stretched to fit into certain criteria in order to help the program work. Frequently, as has been pointed out, you kill innocent victims or at least you certainly maim them with this kind of program.
I am trying to be fair about this matter. I hope the minister will appreciate my concern. My riding is perhaps not affected so possibly I can be objective in this argument. During the debate the minister has heard a great deal of dissatisfaction with these criteria expressed. Members are obviously concerned about their ridings. Almost every week we see news items that an industry has moved out of area B into area C or A because of the incentives offered to do so. Naturally these members are greatly concerned and you can hardly blame a member for saying, let us scrap the whole program because it is not doing much good. This is not what we are saying.
Some provinces have come to the federal government and expressed their disapproval of the program because it was not in harmony with their own plans. I could mention the Maritimes, and there is also dissatisfaction in the province of Quebec where they are trying to establish growth centres based on a different type of criteria, economic planning and
June 3, 1966

the decentralization of industry. Manitoba has expressed its dissatisfaction because it does not like the way the federal government is offering help. The minister can say, as he has said, that the involvement of the federal government in this matter is limited because it can be based only on unemployment. This is a federal responsibility, but economic planning comes within federal jurisdiction to a very limited extent only. I suggest to the minister that perhaps what is called for at this time, in view of the great dissatisfaction which has been expressed in almost every part of Canada, is a federal-provincial conference on the subject of economic planning.
We need a conference to determine how these criteria will be interpreted or if there are better criteria than we have now instead of the limited approach the minister has taken to this subject. I respectfully suggest to the minister that we might first of all get our program in harmony with the plans of the provinces and, second, more in harmony with the whole concept of economic planning, the whole concept of economic feasibility as I used the term the other day. We should be putting industry into those areas where it has a reasonable opportunity for survival, where it can be productive. I resent using industry in this particular fashion to try to cure the short-term unemployment problem. It is admirable that the government wants to cure the short-term problem. I suggest that in the long run, however, if we use industry in this fashion and try to locate industry for this purpose, the long-term problem will be extremely difficult to solve. We will be impairing our ability to be productive and competitive. I think this is something we have to consider seriously.
There is no sense in enticing somebody into an area if the prospects for his long-term survival are not going to be good. When I spoke the other day I perhaps used some fairly strong language to describe this type of program. I do not believe this is the time for strong language. I hope the minister realizes we do not want to hold up these estimates, but the reason this debate has taken place is our deep concern about the criteria. As the hon. member for Timiskaming has pointed out, what do we do about it? How do we, as members of parliament, indicate to the minister that some change has to take place in this method of designation, in establishing these criteria? We have an example here of interfering with the free enterprise system. The untrammelled, free enterprise system has a
Supply-Industry
certain logic of its own, a certain ruthless logic if you like. An industry locates where it suits that industry, without regard to social considerations. We no longer accept this proposition. I am talking about all of us. We accept it to different degrees perhaps, but by and large we think there are social responsibilities to Canada.
We have, as I said, interfered with the workings of the free enterprise system and we have interfered in such a way as to get the worst of both worlds. We get neither the advantages that accrue when businessmen base decisions only on their self-interest nor the advantages which come from proper government economic planning based on getting the best co-operation in certain areas, the best long-range studies and so on, to enable us to do this sort of thing. If we do undertake such a program we will require staff to conduct investigations, economic feasibility studies, land use studies and that kind of thing in order that we will be able to say: This is what we should be doing here; we should be moving secondary industry in with primary industry. Perhaps we have to consider rate of extraction of a resource in an area based on a resource in order to ensure that after 15 or 20 years the resource does not dry up and we are left with a ghost town. You have to do this sort of thing if you are going to have a proper area development program. Perhaps it should not be called an area development program; it should be called an area plan. You cannot do this unilaterally at the federal level. You must do this in conjunction with the provincial governments. You must sit down and work out a national program in harmony with provincial objectives.
It is for this reason we are most anxious that the whole question of designated areas and the establishment of criteria be referred to a committee so that we can have a full discussion of this problem. We cannot solve it in a few hours debate. The problem is too complicated. All we can do in a debate of this kind is to point out our dissatisfaction with the program. The minister has already given us some assurance that he will try to improve the program. I am sure he will do everything in his power to see that the problem is referred to a committee, the proviso being that the committee has the time to study it. I suggest that the problem is of such importance the minister should be prepared to give assurance that a special committee will be set up to ensure a study being made. This program simply is not working the way we

If the committee had an opportunity to vote on this matter I am sure they would decide it should be discussed further. I am not one of those who say the criteria have not been effective. speakerposition: Minister of Industry; Minister of Defence Production
speechtext:
Supply-Defence Production
The Canada-United States defence development and production sharing program, which has become an important part of the department's activities, aims at the optimum utilization of the Canadian and United States defence industrial capabilities by providing equal opportunity for Canadian industry to participate with United States industry on the bases of price, delivery and technical competence in meeting North American defence requirements. About 380 Canadian companies have obtained contracts under the program since its inception in 1959. While government activity has concentrated upon the creation of a climate of opportunity for Canadian industry to compete for United States defence business, the program depends for its success on the continued efforts of Canadian industry.
The agreed objective of the program is to assure maintenance of a long-term balance at the highest practicable level in reciprocal procurement of items of mutual defence interest.
The total of United States defence production sharing business obtained by Canadian companies from 1959 to December, 1965, has amounted to over $1.1 billion. During the calendar year 1964, this business amounted to $167 million and to nearly $260 million in 1965.
Canada's ability to compete in future defence production programs would be lost if we did not continue defence research and development projects in Canada to sustain the technological capability of our industry to produce the complex equipment that is required today. The Canadian government has, since 1959, provided assistance to Canadian companies to undertake development projects for both the United States and other allied defence programs. Financing is carried out on a cost-shared basis between the government, Canadian companies, and the United States or other allied governments.
From the inception of the program to the end of the calendar year 1965, a total of 105 defence development projects have been approved or recommended for government assistance to sustain technological capability in Canadian defence industry. Government expenditures have totalled $69 million. The program to the end of December, 1965, has stimulated $189 million in research and development activity in Canada aimed at meeting the defence requirements of the United States


and other governments. Specific projects supported by the government's development assistance which have resulted in large-scale production for defence export include, in the aircraft field, a small gas turbine engine in the 500 horsepower range which is proving highly successful in military and civil applications; and in the electronics field airborne doppler radar navigation equipment and crash position indicator equipment are examples of items which are selling very well.
Although the department's international activity has been primarily oriented toward the United States, important opportunities are arising in other countries. This stems in part from the fact that unilateral weapon development in NATO and other countries is rapidly giving way to bilateral and multilateral arrangements between countries aimed at making the most effective and economic use of our individual and joint capabilities, replacing competition by co-operation, and conserving industrial and economic resources. Canadian defence industrial planning, therefore, must to an increasing degree be based on allied as well as Canadian military requirements and must be harmonized with the defence development and production plans of those countries with which our military planning is closely associated.
The past year has seen increased emphasis in our overseas international co-operation and bilateral defence trade activities. Departmental representatives have visited a number of European countries and Australia and New Zealand to develop further opportunities for closer collaboration and to survey potential defence export markets. Conversely, defence procurement missions from Britain, France, Germany, Norway, the Netherlands and Australia have visited Canada and we expect that some of these exchanges will result in increased co-operation in defence development and production between our respective countries.
The Anglo-Canadian committee on defence research, development and production, which was formed in 1963, last met in September, 1965. Considerable progress has been made through this committee toward a co-operative approach to the defence requirements of Britain and Canada.

The most recent event of importance in the area of bilateral co-operation was a meeting held early in December 1965 to set the stage for a Franco-Canadian Co-operation Committee on defence research, development and
June 3. 1966	COMMONS
production. As a result, we are at the present time actively employed in considering the precise possibilities of increasing industrial co-operation for defence between France and Canada.
By their very nature, such undertakings are not quickly translated into actual industrial defence projects. Nevertheless, a good start has already been achieved in co-operation with a number of countries and we are in a position to expect that practical results will be more noticeable in the future.
The rising trend of defence equipment exports to overseas countries appears in the statistics of Canadian industrial volume which amounted to some $45 million in 1962, to $53 million in 1963, to nearly $60 million in 1964 and to approximately $68 million in 1965.
The Canadian Commercial Corporation which, as I have indicated, has been incorporated with the Department of Defence Production, continues to assist in the development of trade with other countries by supplying a contract completion service to foreign governments wishing to purchase defence equipment and other supplies in Canada at the government level.

The Department of Defence Production also continues to make progress in the implementation of the recommendations of the Royal Commission on Government Organization relating to the department. As I have already mentioned, the government has approved the establishment within the department of a central purchasing agency to serve all departments and agencies of the federal government other than the commercially-oriented Crown corporations, and has also approved the establishment of the basis for an integrated supply service.
As far as purchasing is concerned, appreciable progress has been made since 1964 when we first integrated the purchasing functions of the Department of Public Printing and Stationery. During the year 1965 the Department of Public Works purchasing responsibilities in regard to furniture, janitorial supplies and maintenance, repair and operating supplies in Ottawa, Toronto and Montreal, were transferred to the Department of Defence Production. The personnel associated with these functions were also transferred to and integrated in the department.

This phase entailed the establishment of a basic organization of six headquarters branches whose specialized technical staff will engage in research and policy formulation in the fields of cataloguing, specifications and standards, regional purchasing, warehousing and distribution, traffic management and quality assurance.

Mr. Chairman, I have little to say about the statement which the minister has made but I hope this is the right time to deal with the Crown Assets Disposal Cor-noration because I have one or two matters to mention in connection with its operations. I have before me a letter written to an Edmonton firm by William C. Gow, salesman, of the Calgary office of the corporation under date of May 5. It reads:
Dear Sir:
In reply to your letter of April 28th, 1966, requesting confirmation that the above named firm is still on the mailing list for surplus vehicles.
We wish to advise that our revised procedure only permits us to sell to distributors, garages and licensed dealers in the automotive trade.
I ask, does this letter refer only to surplus automobile equipment owned by the government? The letter continues:
We are attaching hereto an application form and in the event that you comply with the above conditions would you please complete and return to this office in order that we may review your request and if acceptable return your firm's name to our mailing lists.
Please accept our thanks for bringing this matter to our attention and we anticipate your early reply in this regard.
The firm in question, Midland Mortgage, has been interested in excess buildings, and I have an application in front of me respecting some buildings that have been declared surplus in the Beaverlodge area. This company was interested in their acquisition but I understand it does not qualify to remain on the corporation's list.

I would like to know the minister's definition of licensed dealers. Who is qualified to buy surplus commodities from the government? Are the three categories listed in this letter the only people entitled to buy them? If they are, I cannot see why a garage or automobile distributor would be interested in buying chicken coops, portable hay houses and portable hog houses available at Beaverlodge.
Is the letter incomplete? Does it mean that people in the construction business can buy buildings, people in the automobile business can buy automobiles and people in the office equipment business can buy surplus office equipment? Is that the intent of the department?
What are the criteria under which people can qualify to be put on the list? I understood previously that any legitimate business could be put on the list, but these people in Edmonton have been notified that they do not qualify and therefore are no longer on the list.
I would like to know why the corporation uses the method of advising only those people on its list about the availability of surplus crown assests. I suggest it might be wise to consider the principle followed by provincial governments. Applied to the federal government it would mean that such assets would be advertised in all the national newspapers thus allowing everybody to bid on surplus government commodities. This would eliminate any suggestion of discrimination or political patronage. Every farmer in the west with the necessary resources would then be able to bid on the surplus agricultural buildings at Beaverlodge.
[DOT] (1:20 p.m.)
The provincial governments find this method very effective. They are able to realize a fair price for surplus commodities. I suggest to the minister that he should consider using that system rather than the present one because when Midland Mortgage, as I have mentioned, is taken off the list for very little reason one might think that there is patronage involved with respect to who should and who should not be on the list. How are people put on the list? Are you invited? Do you answer? No one really knows. Do you go to your member of parliament and say: "I want to get on the list"? How does a contractor in the city of Edmonton, for example, make inquiries concerning how he can get on the list? Does he communicate with the people in Crown Assets Disposal Corporation? How is
June 3, 1966

it done? I should like to have an answer from the minister in this regard. In view of the many cancellations in respect of the old and existing lists, I think it would clear up a very important question in the minds of some of the business people, particularly in my area.

speakerposition: Minister of Industry; Minister of Defence Production
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I do not know the circumstances surrounding the Midland Mortgage Placements Company Limited removal from the list, as the hon. gentleman puts it. I hope to have that information a little later. Let me say, however, that in general Crown Assets Disposal Corporation is charged with the task of disposing of surplus commodities entrusted to it for disposal. These are commodities surplus to the requirements of the Crown. In the disposal of these commodities the corporation endeavours to realize, through sale, the best possible price for the taxpayer. Obviously the return to the taxpayer is a net of the sale price realized less the cost of selling.
Through experience over the years Crown Assets Disposal Corporation has concluded that in respect of some commodities it is better economics to carry on business selling to wholesalers than it is to try to get themselves into the retail business. In respect of other items it is better, and indeed essential, to do the retailing job themselves. In the case of buildings or properties, for instance, they operate as retailers; they advertise as widely as possible and send out invitations to tender or bid in respect of the properties. Anyone who wishes to put in a bid is free to do so and indeed is encouraged to do so. In respect of certain commodities which may recur, however, notably scrap metal and scrap clothing, and which periodically appear on their list for disposal, they have developed a pattern of selling to the trade. They have discovered it is productive of a much better return to sell to the trade for disposal and resale than it is to conduct a series of public auctions or engage in whatever other method there may be of retailing the commodities.
It costs more to sell to the trade at retail than it does at wholesale and the net is higher on occasion, as has been shown by experience, by selling to the wholesale trade. This is in relation to scrap. In relation to any surplus commodity, however, whether it be buildings, property or movables, anybody is entitled to put in a bid. The high bidder, who is financially responsible, of course-and I must always make that exception-gets the sale. I have one qualification only to make to
Supply-Defence Production that and it is in relation to surplus motor vehicles. This is a special case. Apart from that anyone is entitled to bid and the high bidder makes the purchase. So in so far as items other than motor cars are concerned Midland Mortgage Placement Company Limited is free to bid and free to buy anything and everything. The only things demanded of them are (a) financial responsibility and (b) the high bid.
In order to encourage interest in bidding Crown Assets Disposal Corporation has a list of people who in the past have been in the habit of buying and who have demonstrated a real interest in buying as distinct from merely curiosity. Anyone who has demonstrated or any corporation which has demonstrated a real interest in buying is put on a list and the list is circulated. Duplicates of the public notices of sale are sent to the person or the corporation to make sure that the advertisement is not overlooked. In this way it is drawn to their attention in the hope that they will bid. In order for anyone to get on this list all we ask is that they exhibit something more than mere curiosity so that the Crown is not put to the expense of sending out these notices to somebody who never is going to make a purchase. People who in the past have been receiving these notices and have never done anything about them are crossed off. This is the list to which I think the hon. member has been referring.
If Midland Mortgage Placement Company Limited is serious about bidding, Crown Assets Disposal Corporation is delighted to send them notices of invitation to tender in the hope that these will produce real bids.

With the exception of
automobiles.

speakerposition: Minister of Industry; Minister of Defence Production
speechtext:
Yes. The question of automobiles is another story. Recently the Department of Defence Production has undertaken the task of acquiring automobiles to meet all the requirements in the government service and not merely in the Department of National Defence. This gives rise to the problem of how to dispose of the vehicles for which the new vehicles generally are replacements. Most of the new vehicles are replacements rather than original equipment to fill a need which never existed before. So there is a turnover problem. Previously, under the old practice of allowing individual departments and agencies to make their own deals in any way they could with any dealer whom they chose, this problem of disposing of surplus
June 3, 1966

Supply-Defence Production vehicles did not arise because part of the purchase price involved in getting a new car was taken in the old one.
We have explored quite extensively with the trade, from the Crown's point of view, the most advantageous technique by which to dispose of the surplus cars. The various techniques which occur to me offhand are private sales such as one might make through a newspaper advertisement in the personal columns, public auctions, sales to individual dealers on a negotiated basis or by inviting dealers and the general public to bid, or sales to the wholesalers again on a negotiated basis. There are many alternatives which present themselves. One has to arrive at a device or system which will meet in the best possible way the situation where 30 cars have to be disposed of at one time in the city of Toronto or one car at Yellowknife in the Northwest Territories. Obviously it is difficult to have a uniform, single technique which is going to cover all of these situations.
[DOT] (1:30 p.m.)
We have come to the conclusion, and so far this is only experimental until we see how it works, that the best way to do this, in order not to disrupt the trade and produce instability of prices by dumping large numbers of cars on occasion on the retail market, is to deal only with the trade, namely, dealers, in the hope that we will obtain a continuing interest and market with a consequential stability of the market. That is our approach and it is for that reason that Midland Mortgage, which does not by its name sound like a second hand car business, would not be invited to bid for used cars.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to ask a question because of the statement that the general methods employed by the corporation have pretty well been maintained over the years. Perhaps I misunderstood the minister and, if so, I hope he will correct me.
In 1964 the public accounts committee had some anxiety about the methods employed by the corporation, its disposal procedures and techniques. This anxiety was particularly applicable to certain negotiations and transactions which took place in regard to the Department of National Defence. That committee made some recommendations in its seventh report in 1964 to the effect that sales inspection procedures followed by Crown Assets Disposal Corporation should be revised with a view to improving sales techniques. Some time in November of 1965 the minister

replied that steps had been taken or were being taken by the corporation to revise and upgrade its operating instructions in the area of pre-sales analyses and inspections. He also stated that the corporation proposed to undertake a more aggressive sales campaign in such areas as market research and analysis to develop new methods of improving its solicitation lists and explore ways and means of interesting new and substantial merchandising outlets. I was interested in this in view of what the hon. member for Edmonton East said about developing new methods of improving the solicitation list.
Can the minister tell us whether, after his statement of February and in line with what he said, these new techniques have actually been instituted and whether the corporation is making progress in this regard? Has the corporation been successful as a result of these new techniques in displaying a somewhat better method of developing solicitation lists than was displayed at least to the public accounts committee when it investigated this matter?

speakerposition: Minister of Industry; Minister of Defence Production
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I did not and do not want to give the impression that Crown Assets Disposal Corporation is unchanging or unchangeable. What I really should have said, in relation to the hon. member's question, is that sales to the public and to the highest bidder and realizing the highest returns to the Crown are objectives that do not change. As to the means of achieving these objectives, improvements undoubtedly can be effected.
The views and advice of the public accounts committee have been accepted with enthusiasm by the corporation and a number of them have been put into effect. Others are in the process of being incorporated, but I am not sure that others are entirely appropriate to the degree that the public accounts committee suggested. Considering the size of the Crown Assets Disposal's operation, one can very quickly understand that as a sales organization it could bankrupt itself by spending too much money on marketing investment. I am sure the hon. member will appreciate that. Certainly a little more in the way of marketing analysis than has perhaps been the case in the past would be and has proven useful in respect of Crown Assets.

Would the hon. minister
make some reference to the phrase "solicitation lists"?

speakerposition: Minister of Industry; Minister of Defence Production
speechtext:
Solicitation can be done in a number of ways. As I have indicated, one is by public advertising in newspapers and other media, and this costs a certain sum of money in terms of the impact one creates. Another method is by direct mail. I suppose those are the two most important ones. At the present time Crown Assets is employing both, and from time to time in respect of particular commodities more of one and less of the other or more of the other and less of the one proves to be the most efficacious in achieving effective price bid solicitations. The corporation does want to get as much interest in what it is selling and as many bids as possible, having in mind always that one must not allow the cost of the solicitation to become unreasonable in terms of the advantage obtained through having a few more bids. I am sure the hon. gentleman appreciates that fact.
As the public accounts committee has pointed out, perhaps not enough emphasis has been placed on active solicitation at some additional expense. Perhaps this would be desirable and I think it is in the process of taking place.
