speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the Liberal Party; Chief Government Whip's assistant; Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: This concludes the estimates of the Department of Defence Production. We shall now study the estimates of the Department of Citizenship and Immigration.

1. General administration including the promotion of a program for the employment of the older worker; the promotion of programs for combating seasonal unemployment; the organization and use of workers for farming and related industries; and the manpower consultative service, $3,913,500.

Mr. Chairman, I am sorry I was slightly late. I just had a sandwich so I would be able to read this statement.
TTranslation]
Mr. Chairman, in the course of the next weeks and later in the session, the house will have before it at various times the consideration of the plans of my department. As a result, my statement will be restricted to the estimates and general remarks indicating our major aim and the projects we are trying to carry out.
May I first be permitted to pay tribute, whatever their political persuasion, to my predecessors in the Department of Citizenship
DEBATES	5939
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration and Immigration and in the Department of Labour. I should also like to note the devotion of the officials of these two departments, particularly during the past few months, while the changeover and the new direction was being prepared.
The functions assigned to the Department of Citizenship and Immigration as well as the establishment of a new department which will direct manpower policies and programs at the national level would seem, I feel, to make up a most interesting program, the importance of which must be stated.

Successive governments have developed a variety of programs designed to improve the utilization of our human resources. There are many good programs already in existence and the department of manpower will not be launched with the idea that all present programs need to be replaced.
[DOT] (1:40 p.m.)
We do believe that existing programs can be made much more effective within a single agency and that agency can also plan, develop and implement whatever new programs are required. I know that members fully appreciate why manpower policy has become so important. We all recognize that the increasing rate at which the world is changing requires in people an adaptability never before necessary in our history, and that in our society the pace of change itself is accelerated. We cannot arrest these changes. We must accept a new pace, understand it, master it and profit from it.
The estimates you are being asked to approve bring together in the one department the national employment service, the immigration service, the training, rehabilitation, mobility and winter employment programs, the manpower consultative service and the groups responsible for economic and social research and labour market analysis. All the active manpower programs are to be the responsibility of one strong, integrated, national manpower service with offices across Canada organized to give a full range of advice, counsel and service to worker and employer.

I believe that concerning the organization and the arrangement of the staff, the progress achieved tends to increase the efficiency of the department. We can already rely upon several skilled and devoted employees. In the
June 3, 1966
5940	COMMONS
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration years to come, our first aim will be not to initiate new plans but rather to get ready to increase the results of present programs, to improve on their quality, to make them more accessible to those who will need them and to render services where required.
Such is the state of mind with which we are inspired in setting up a manpower service based on the organization that other bodies and other departments have already created. Integrated as to its purpose, the manpower service will be highly decentralized in its organization. It will be concerned with the different needs in various areas and yarious industries. Its scope and objectives will be national, taking the regional needs into account. Furthermore, it will operate in close co-operation with the provincial governments.
The five regional directors will be responsible for all federal manpower programs, for the National Employment Service as well as for the numerous other work performed up to now in the department at Ottawa. The regional directors will be under the assistant deputy minister, but they will have at hand and under their direct orders, experts and specialists who will enable them to keep informed on the needs of industry, to work with the provincial governments and to support much more closely the local manpower offices. The personnel of the N.E.S. is much smaller that the staff authorized by parliament. We have an enormous job ahead of us, in the recruiting as well as in the organization. Our own staff training will be of major importance.

If I were asked, Mr. Chairman, to state the department's current objectives in their simplest terms, I would reply that we simply intend building an organization for doing things for people. Our purpose is to assist the growth of Canada by helping people to get better jobs and to do better jobs or broaden the opportunities that are open to them. Our concern is with the challenge of the present. It can all be said very simply, but I think that we all realize it may be very difficult and will require a complex and competent organization of dedicated and understanding people.
Immigration has been integrated with other elements of our manpower program in the new department. This is as it should be because immigration can in that way make its full contribution to the economic growth. I emphasize, however, that manpower is more
[Mr. Marchand.l

than economics. It is people. In putting immigration into the manpower department there is every realization that the role of immigration is not to be measured solely in economic terms nor as a precise response to manpower requirements alone at any given time.
The shortages in our manpower requirements, especially with regard to skilled or professional people, is of vast importance in shaping immigration programs, but there are other important factors as well, including the social and cultural ones. Canada's social and cultural development has benefited greatly from immigration over the years. That fact is and will remain in the forefront of our plans and our work toward a wise and comprehensive immigration policy.

Some people have claimed that to place immigration under manpower could be conducive to its being planned solely in terms of our economic needs, without due regard to the social and humanitarian considerations which should inspire it. It was feared in certain quarters that entrusting immigration to a department preoccupied with employment would lead to a timid and unsteady program, amenable to the least fluctuations of our economy and employment in Canada.
I cannot accept the idea that economic and manpower planning could harm immigration. On the contrary, an active manpower policy requires an active immigration policy capable of increasing its efficiency and promoting growth and prosperity in Canada.

Because immigration is such a vital factor in Canadian growth and development, because it affects so many lives, it is essential that immigration be carefully planned and executed. It means that to the best of our ability immigration must be administered in accordance with the basic principles of justice and humanity which Canadians demand in their national endeavours. The reason immigration and manpower should be so intimately related is precisely that they both are concerned with human resources. In operational terms, as the committee knows, there has been a great deal of work done in the immigration service in recent years to modernize and reorganize its facilities and strengthen its staff. I venture to say that in many ways it is ahead of the rest of the department and we are leaning heavily on
June 3, 196G

the experience and involvement of the immigration service in developing the department as a whole.
I have taken more time than I intended but I did wish to speak today in terms of the principles which are motivating the department. The needs are very great. We have high objectives and some of the organizational problems may be quite difficult. In no sense would I wish to convey to the committee that manpower has now become an exact science. I am looking forward to suggestions and will be glad to give or secure answers to any questions that hon. members may have regarding these estimates.

I should probably make clear that our estimates are presented to you in a provisional form as we are determining the responsibilities and duties of the new department. The estimates for 1965-66 respecting tasks previously entrusted to the Department of Labour are indicated only where all these tasks have been transferred and when a separate vote had been written down for this purpose in past year estimates. Where no amount is indicated for 1965-66, the vote of the previous year is transferred to the estimates of the Department of Labour.
I hope, Mr. Chairman, the hon. members of the house will accede to my request and approve the estimates before us.
[DOT] (1:50 p.m.)

Mr. Chairman, these estimates reflect the as yet unconsummated marriage of immigration and labour. My desire to preserve the chastity of each is well known to members of the committee but it appears there is no option but to relax, if not to enjoy. And so, sir, I propose this afternoon to deal mainly with immigration and citizenship. Other members of the opposition will deal with matters related to manpower.
This is the second time in just over three months that the estimates dealing with immigration and citizenship have been before the committee of supply. The intervening brief three month period has supplied ample evidence, as I said at that time, that the department has suffered greatly as the result of being under four ministers during a period of less than three years. I wish to say that I do not think any of the ministers, least of all the present one, has had an opportunity to take firm control and become the active directing
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration head of the department of immigration. I sincerely regret the game of musical chairs that has been played in respect of the portfolio of citizenship and immigration and I think that the public interest has suffered thereby.
I know the Prime Minister is unrepentant in this respect and I only hope that in the short life of the present government the hon. member for Quebec West will be given the uninterrupted opportunity to become a firm directing head of the department and to bring into effect vigorous policies related to immigration.
First I would like to speak of citizenship before those estimates are placed under the Secretary of State. I have already stated my grave reservations about this change and I will not repeat them. However, I think that in no other aspect of the department has the unique faculty of this government for procrastination and legislative indolence been so amply demonstrated. What has happened to the once urgent and long promised amendments to the Canadian Citizenship Act? What is the history of these amendments forecast at one stage by the hon. member for Papineau? Would you believe that in those early days when the Prime Minister was seeking to excite the bold and challenge the daring the first Speech from the Throne delivered on May 16, 1963 contained the following phrase:
A change in the citizenship act will be proposed to ensure full equality of rights for all Canadian citizens wherever they were born.
I want hon. members to note those words. On hearing them parliamentarians of all parties gave three cheers. Their chorus of approval was premature. No final parliamentary action was taken while the hon. member for Papineau was minister of citizenship and immigration. So what happened? In the Speech from the Throne made on February 18, 1964, the following sentence appeared:
You will be asked to consider amendments to the citizenship act which will ensure full equality of rights for all Canadian citizens wherever they were born.
Was any action taken? Of course not. In this first session of the new parliament, which opened on January 18 of this year, the author of the Speech from the Throne was highly original. He put it this way:
My government will propose legislation to amend the Canadian Citizenship Act, in order to ensure equality of rights for all citizens.

Supply-Citizenship and Immigration
What a travesty of parliamentary leadership and action these three quotations represent. What is the result at this session? Parliament has been in session for four and a half months and the hon. member for Quebec West has done nothing to bring forward amendments to the Canadian Citizenship Act. If they were ready for introduction in 1963 as forecast by the Speech from the Throne, why could they not have been put on the order paper in January of this year?
If the amendments are what I expect them to be, we on this side of the house will put them through within a matter of minutes. However, parliamentary approval cannot be given to legislation forecast by a government which, with its typical languor or should I say somnolence neglects even to introduce it.
I do not like the legislative game being played of three successive Speeches from the Throne containing precisely the same forecast of legislation. If the government is serious in its intentions, let it act now. I say to the hon. gentleman: Introduce this bill, put it on the order paper tonight, not next week. The fact is that the government has no real interest in these amendments except as a carrot held out politically to influence naturalized Canadian citizens.
I put it to the minister now, and I have no doubt I will have to repeat it to the Secretary of State later, that it is time they stopped sitting on their hands; it is time they went to work to put into effect legislative reforms which were once so dear to the heart of the hon. gentleman from Bonavista-Twillingate. I think I can forecast what will happen. The next Speech from the Throne will contain the same pious hope. This is one prediction which I hope will not be fulfilled.
In my view this country has been lax and dilatory in its citizenship program. Last year I had the opportunity to visit Australia where I was vividly impressed with how much greater was their sense of national identity, their pride in nationhood, in the greatness of a wonderful and aggressive nation which, however, does not equal this land either in resources or in potential. We are throwing away the advantage that we have in this country.
Of course, I do not believe in jingoistic indoctrination but I do believe most earnestly that we are not giving sufficient support to the dedicated work of the officials of the


citizenship branch, nor is there sufficient coordination of the federal and provincial activities in the field of citizenship and of both with the educational systems.
Today, for the first time in a hundred years the survival of this nation is imperilled, and I believe a massive effort in the field of citizenship is imperative. Our philosophical objectives and our targets as a nation, our right to be proud of and to respect our various traditions and heritages should be delineated and promoted. Nothing less than a massive effort by the citizenship branch will be sufficient. I hope that when the minister replies he will tell us what the government plans in this field, what he plans in the field of citizenship education and registration. Is sufficient effort being made to encourage eligible persons to apply for citizenship? What are the plans for the establishment of additional courts of Canadian citizenship? What is being done to make Canadian citizenship ceremonies more impressive and more warmhearted?
[DOT] (2:00 p.m.)
From time to time I hear complaints about one or two judges of the courts of Canadian citizenship displaying sharp or at least unsympathetic attitudes to applicants. Personally I hope the present minister, or the Secretary of State when it becomes a matter for that minister, will talk turkey to any judges guilty of such conduct, for nowhere is it so important to have warmhearted understanding, friendly human treatment, as in these courts. Any judge who wraps himself in his judicial cloak and speaks and deals with applicants in the fashion of a harassed magistrate in a metropolitan police court is doing a grave disservice. One judge whose friendliness and warmhearted understanding is frequently commented upon to me is the local Ottawa and Carleton judge, Judge John A. Dawson. His broad knowledge of people, his general affection for all men, his lack of side or pomposity, his ability to combine firmness with charity, these qualities which he has demonstrated amply are qualities which should be emulated by all citizenship judges.
I should like now to say a word about another aspect of citizenship which concerns me greatly, namely, the handling of the so-called security cases. The minister and all his predecessors in this chamber will know the problem. It is one which caused me the gravest concern of any in my brief sojourn in the department. I confess I agonized over these files and wrestled with my conscience which I could never satisfy. The existing
June 3, 1966

system, I am certain, is wrong, blatantly wrong, and had I remained minister tor a month or two longer the system and the principles behind it would have been drastically altered. I think perhaps that is as far as I am entitled to go in the light of my Privy Councillor's oath. However, I urge most earnestly upon the minister and the Prime Minister that the terms of reference of the proposed royal commission on security be drafted to include a provision for consideration and report on this particular aspect of security. The minister will find in the departmental files a secret memorandum written by me at the end of my ministry, in my own indecipherable handwriting, expressing my views. I venture to submit that those views so expressed might be considered now by the minister and later by the royal commission.
The depriving of Canadian citizenship of persons who have been in Canada for lengthy periods, and who hold political views which are entirely legal in this country, is a most serious matter in a freedom loving nation.
I should like to turn to a discussion of immigration. As the committee knows, I am an unrepentant expansionist in connection with immigration policy. It is because of that that I confess I am a bit appalled at the audacity of the government in bringing forward these estimates without a white paper being presented, without even a prior acknowledgement of the existence of the Sedgwick report, with no statement of government policy about its important recommendations and without any action to revise and update the Immigration Act. I use the word "audacity" and I think it is an effrontery to parliament; yes, and it is arrogant. The government and the minister have been simply swinging the lead. I have no apology for saying to the minister that he has been swinging the lead in this respect. There have been questions in the house by various members on the imminence of a white paper, when would there be a statement of government policy, and he has simply avoided the issue.
His latest gem was a suggestion that the new policy would be announced soon to enable the hon. member for Carleton to sleep more peacefully. Well, sir, my sleep is unimportant.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
speechtext: I should like to ask the hon. member whether he swung the lead when he was minister and failed to bring in any changes to the Immigration Act?

I will deal precisely with that situation. I took specific action which is now bearing fruit. This will be found in the files, and I recommended that we should have an expansionist policy in immigration. My friend knows that. He knows that as soon as I took command of that department I went out to the public and sought to gain support for an expansionist immigration policy.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
speechtext: But there was no change in the act when the hon. member was in charge of the department.

I will deal precisely with that before I finish. I will tell the hon. gentleman that the regulations were amended and a specific deadline date established when we would then advance the amendments to the Immigration Act.
Somehow, sir, we were discussing the question of my sleep. I say my sleep is unimportant compared with the long Rip Van Winkle sleep of this government. Not even a snore disturbs their slumbers. The hon. member for Vancouver Centre in my view is a man who really believes in immigration. If he had been kept in the immigration portfolio he would have done a tremendous job. However, he was shifted into a portfolio in which I do not believe he is extremely happy, and this is one of the major regrets that we in this house have.
The white paper on immigration was first mentioned on December 31, 1964, when the Prime Minister promised it at the beginning of the next session. Well, two sessions later we are still awaiting it. Four ministers have been unable to persuade the cabinet to adopt a white paper. The fault is not with the officials of the department. The two gentlemen over there know very well that the department can produce all the necessary material and have it ready within 48 hours, if the minister knew what he wanted to establish as a policy or if the cabinet would come to grips for a change with this important phase of our national life.
Now, sir, I think that actually this committee should refuse to pass these estimates without a white paper. Until I hear what the minister has to say about the inordinate delays that have occurred in connection with
June 3, 1966

Supply-Citizenship and Immigration this white paper, I reserve the right to move an amendment to reduce these estimates.
What about the Sedgwick report? We have not heard a word from the minister when lie introduced his estimates. The original section of that report dealing with ships' deserters has been in the hands of the government for 13 months. What has the government done? What is the attitude of the government? Can the government not make up its collective mind on this? We cannot get an answer out of the minister concerning the problem of Yugoslav ship deserters about which the hon. member for Ontario has inquired. What does the minister plan to do? Will he follow the Sedgwick formula? Has he now some new magic to deal with the problem? I am not unaware of the difficulties, and there is a member sitting close to the hon. gentleman who knows that. I submit to the minister that a difficult problem does not just disappear. This stalling is no substitute for initiative. When he replies I should like the minister to tell us precisely what he proposes to do with these Yugoslav deserters. What is his plan for the future of these people? He has had the report before him for 13 months, and I think this committee cannot grant the minister a permanent reprieve from decision.
Why did the minister not tell us today when he introduced his estimates about his policy in respect of part II of the Sedgwick report? I think it is a most significant document. I want to ask the minister certain specific questions and I hope he will make specific answers. Does he agree that a genuine appeal should be established in all cases from the making of an order for deportation? What is he doing to bring this about? Is he contemplating, as Mr. Sedgwick suggests, that he might establish a procedure of "exclusion orders"? Is he contemplating a new class of deportable persons, namely, persons in Canada who counsel or abet others to remain in the country illegally? What are his plans for an immigration appeal board? Does he propose to give it final discretion or does he support my view, contrary to Mr. Sedgwick, that a limited residual authority should remain with the minister?
[DOT] (2:10 p.m.)
These are genuine questions to which I think the committee is entitled to have answers. They might properly have been answered in a white paper. How can the minister expect the committee to vote him supply without these answers? What are his plans for the more than 20,000 people who are in

Canada illegally, according to Mr. Sedgwick who, indeed, adds that more are arriving daily? Does he propose an amnesty or moratorium?
Mr. Sedgwick had the courage to state his views clearly about sponsored immigration. These views, in which I do not concur, have caused consternation among a number of ethnic groups. What is the minister's policy? Does he propose to adopt Mr. Sedgwick's proposal to limit sponsorship to spouses and dependent minor children of Canadian citizens or landed immigrants? If he does, it will throw havoc into established patterns of immigration from Italy, Greece, Portugal and Hong Kong.
I think there must be great concern, Mr. Chairman, about sponsorships in some of the ethnic classes where in fact sponsorship exceeds the process of selection by our own immigration officers. But what does the minister propose? I think we are entitled to know this today.
What does the minister think about the processes and procedures of exempting by order in council a considerable number of individuals each week or so, or whenever an order in council can be passed, who are inadmissible under the regulations, a procedure so strongly condemned by Mr. Sedgwick? This, we remember, is how Hal Banks became a landed immigrant.
The Sedgwick report deals basically and fundamentally with all these issues. But a pigeonholed report is almost worse than no report at all. I want the minister to be frank and open with the committee and to give us the facts. I plead with him today not to try to rely on philosophical or brush-off answers to these very practical and realistic questions which I have put to him.
I ask him to tell us now to what extent the government is co-operating with the government of Manitoba in their free passage program to attract immigrants to that province. How will this program operate? Will it be attempted on a national scale?
I think, Mr. Chairman, that the committee should know that we simply cannot compete in the United Kingdom with the financial allurements offered by Australia. Nor do I think we can compete in other European countries. Three years ago I observed in Austria through a friend, the head of the Australian immigration mission to Austria, Mr. Fred Ordish, the manner in which that office in Vienna seeks to assist desirable immigrants to Australia. I only wish we gave
June 3, 19C6
our officers abroad equivalent support and assistance.
Then, sir, what of the proposed revision of the Immigration Act to which the hon. member for Parkdale referred? The previous government had specific plans for a full-out revision and then decided that as a first step a completely new set of regulations with major policy changes should be adopted as an interim measure. That government announced that as soon as a reasonable period of experimentation with these regulations had passed a full revision of the act would be undertaken. I do not know whether this has been forgotten. The regulations have now been in operation for five years.
Five years?

Yes, I think so, or is it
four? No, it is five. The period of experimentation, I suggest, is over. I submit that a full revision of this obsolete, archaic Immigration Act is overdue. I would ask the minister whether he would consider referring the draft act to the standing committee which could hear witnesses, get information and give all those interested the opportunity to make presentations. I ask him today to come to grips with the problem, because I am getting tired of drift and procrastination as a general instrument of national policy.
The minister has undoubtedly been able to review the Edith Ferguson report for the international institute of metropolitan Toronto, which has condemned apparently in vigorous terms governmental inactivity, especially at the federal level, in the provision of funds, programs and co-ordination for immigrant education. I have not yet been able to secure a full text of the report but the report in the Globe and Mail of May 30, 1966, disturbs one in respect of settlement arrangements. The report states in part:
The study suggests that outdated attitudes toward education and toward immigrants are combining to hamper the Canadian economy.
Blame for a lack of funds to remedy the situation is laid almost entirely to the federal government.
The report goes on:
Federal immigration officers overseas fail to tell the prospective immigrant "that he will be expected to learn the language of the community where he settles, that unskilled jobs are likely to grow scarcer and that it would be advisable for him to consider the acquisition of some specific type of skill".
She said the federal government is also remiss in making available only a single man's allowance to unemployed men registered in program 5 (a plan in which immigrants can take English lessons)
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration who are supporting families in the old countries; another injustice is that no government subsidized scheme exists similar to program 5 for employed persons who wish to upgrade themselves.
"Recent arrivals feel they have been misled by Department of Immigration officials who did not make the true state of affairs known to them at the time of application. When they write home or return home, they tell their experiences to other prospective immigrants."
There are many interesting statements in this report, including a number of specific recommendations. Doubtless the minister has studied the report in detail, and I would ask him to comment on these recommendations in some detail when he replies.
Earlier, Mr. Chairman, I said that I was an unregenerate expansionist in immigration policy. Canada requires a much larger population. A policy of genuine national development involves population planning or at least the development of basic concepts as to the quality, optimum size and rate of growth of population.

speechtext: Would the hon. gentleman permit a question?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration
speechtext: Does the hon. gentleman agree that during the latter years of the administration of which he was a member and minister of citizenship and immigration a severe cut-back was made in the budget which did not allow any real promotional program in immigration? As a result there was a marked decrease in immigration into this country during the latter years of that administration.

I say to the hon.
gentleman that as soon as I took over the portfolio of immigration I sought to have a marked increased in the amount of money which was made available, and I succeeded in getting that marked increase. I started a genuine promotional program abroad which, by reason of the attitude of the labour department toward immigration, had been cut up to that time. It is just because of this that I am so concerned now at the marriage of labour and immigration. I saw at once that it was from the labour section that the influences against immigration were being exerted. That is why I have described the new department of manpower and immigration as a department warring within itself. At least there could be war among two cabinet ministers under previous circumstances, but now it is a war within the department.

The hon. gentleman has access to the facts, and I would say to him that he will find the complete situation described in the files of the department, showing the policy statement which was set forth for the year 1963 and for future years.
In conclusion, Mr. Chairman, all I want to say is this. I have expressed in previous times my view that we as a nation should set specific national objectives. What I have said many times is that one national objective should be, on a long-range basis, an inflow of immigrants of at least 1 per cent of population per annum, subject to adjustment within the limits of .75 to 1.25 per cent of population. If we establish a clear target such as this we can avoid the drawbacks of annual immigration planning. For under annual immigration planning, facilities cannot be maintained abroad, particularly in terms of trained staff to carry out the immigration programs. The stabilization of immigration policy will permit the maintenance of a trained immigration staff able to cope with reasonable problems and emergency situations.
[DOT] (2:20 p.m.)
That is why I say this white paper is so much overdue. I appeal to the minister now to state policy forthwith and to proceed ahead with the greatest of vigour. The minister, I know, takes satisfaction in the rising immigration statistics. I take satisfaction in those also. I say to the hon. member for Hamilton East that this increase is the result of policies adopted in the autumn of 1962 and early winter of 1963. Governmental policy has really coasted since that time.
Sir, Canada needs more population. We need the cultural advantages of the best immigrants from other lands. We need the continuing stimulus to our economy. Let us go out to promote immigration. Mr. Chairman, there are three points in respect of which I should like to comment while we are discussing vote No. 1 of the estimates of the Department of Citizenship and Immigration. The first point I wish to make is more in the nature of a question than a comment. I have raised this point on two or three occasions in the past but nothing has been done about it in spite of promises contained annually in Speeches from the Throne. It has to do with proposed amendments to the "Canadian Citizenship Act which will ensure full equality of rights for all Canadian citizens wherever they were born."
The party sitting to the right of Mr. Speaker has been in power for a little better than three years, since April of 1963, during which time we have had four ministers of immigration. When you ask why the minister does not do something about the promises contained in Speeches from the Throne to the effect that an amendment will be made to the citizenship act the answer is always that the minister was not in office when the promises were made. It seems that in order to avoid putting into effect the promises contained in the Speeches from the Throne, the government changes the minister. I do not think that is good enough, because a Speech from the Throne is read by the Governor General


who has been the same honourable gentleman since this party came into power.
In the riding that has been good enough to elect me to parliament there is located the town of Weston with a population of about 10,000. Very shortly after my election to parliament I received an urgent letter from Canadian citizens of Italian birth who were greatly exorcised over the fact that they had gone to Italy for a visit and because of the cost of living there and the number of relatives they had in Italy had stayed for a number of years. They understood that before coming back to Canada they had to have their passports validated, but when they sent their passports to the Canadian embassy in Rome they were informed they had lost their Canadian citizenship because they had stayed out of Canada for so many years during which time their passports had not been validated. These people were desperate because they had Canadian-born sons and daughters in this country and wished to return. They had renounced their Italian citizenship in favour of Canadian citizenship and were glad to have done so. They were informed by the Canadian embassy that they had forfeited their Canadian citizenship because they had stayed out of Canada for a certain length of time.
I immediately took the matter up with the minister of immigration and I am happy to say that these people received the utmost co-operation and their passports were validated, re-establishing them once again as Canadian citizens.
This episode occurred two or three years ago at a time when a tremendous decision was rendered unanimously by the supreme court of the United States whereby a German born wife of a United States citizen, who had been a member of the United States armed forces in Germany when he married, could not lose her citizenship as a result of the soldier-husband and wife returning to Germany after the war to the village or town in which his wife was born and raised. The United States supreme court ruled that this German native born citizen, having renounced her German citizenship and accepted United States citizenship, could not be deprived of her United States citizenship unless she herself voluntarily renounced it in favour of citizenship of another country. That was a tremendous decision rendered unanimously, and it represents a mountain peak of freedom for United States citizens.

I was referring to Lord Thomson of Fleet, who has lost his Canadian citizenship, I say temporarily because his citizenship should be restored to him by the Canadian cabinet. The Nickle resolution states that titles should not be conferred on Canadian citizens ordinarily resident or domiciled in Canada, and heaven knows Lord Thomson is not ordinarily resident or domiciled in Canada. But when the member for Lotbiniere asked the question last Friday he set up a chain of thought that some of us have been developing throughout the week.
It comes to this. How is it that certain prominent Canadians can be sworn into the privy council of, shall I say, a foreign government and not lose their Canadian citizenship, whereas if another Canadian citizen is sworn into the parliament of the same foreign country he loses his Canadian citizenship? How is it possible for a Canadian citizen to be honoured by a foreign government, shall I say, and then return with the title of "right honourable"? I do not need to name those who carry the title of "right honourable" around these halls or in this Dominion of Canada; there are a few of them. But the question that comes up is: If Lord Thomson could not become a member of the British House of Lords without the recommendation of the cabinet of Canada to the Queen of Canada, or the recommendation of the government of Great Britain to the Queen of Great Britain, who recommends those Canadian citizens who wind up with the title of "right honourable"? Does the Queen reach out and say to certain Canadians, "Of my own volition I give you the courtesy title of right honourable"?
Her Majesty could not do that to Mr. Roy Thomson, a native born Canadian from Toronto. She was told, "You cannot honour him without a recommendation from the cabinet of the section of the Commonwealth of which he is a citizen". And since no such recommendation came forward from Canada he

secured a recommendation from another section of the Commonwealth, but still remains a British subject and still remains Toronto born, but is no longer a citizen of Canada. It is a mighty fine distinction, if you ask me, between "right honourable" and a knighthood, a baronetcy or a title in the nobility. But the Nickle resolution distinctly reads:
Most Gracious Sovereign.
We, Your Majesty's most dutiful and loyal subjects, the House of Commons of Canada in parliament assembled, humbly approach Your Majesty, praying that Your Majesty may be graciously pleased:
(a) To refrain hereafter from conferring any title of honour or titular distinction upon any of your subjects domiciled or ordinarily resident in Canada-

If it is a titular distinction, those who hold it should yield their Canadian citizenship in the same manner as Roy Thomson was forced to voluntarily give up his Canadian citizenship in order to accept a title in the nobility of Great Britain. It is an angle that I think the minister of citizenship should follow through, and se why it is that we have right honourables in Canada who are still considered Canadian citizens, but when you have a Toronto-born Canadian like Roy Thomson enjoying the title and perquisites of Lord Thomson of Fleet, he is no longer a Canadian citizen.

Mr. Chairman, as several members pointed out this afternoon, I am in favour of an extensive and systematic immigration for Canada. I feel, however, that our immigration policy should take into account the situation of the Canadian economy and labour market, not exclusively but inclusively, among other factors.
We are told sometimes that we should follow the example of the United States. It was somewhat the basis of the argument put forward by the member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert). As a matter of fact, I thought his intervention contained the same type of argument. According to that argument, we should follow the American policy, that is, accept the greatest possible number of immigrants, with a view to extending our domestic
June 3, 1966

Supply-Citizenship and Immigration market and eventually bringing about prosperity.
Now, Mr. Chairman, it should be kept in mind that conditions in 1966 are not the same as those which prevailed when massive immigration took place in the United States. The professional requirements of the labour class, when the United States allowed massive immigration were not similar to those existing today.
When I joined the trade union movement, probably 30 per cent of labour was unskilled and could easily be absorbed by industry. Nowadays, this ratio has fallen to 10 per cent and keeps going down. At a time when our efforts are directed towards professional and technical training, we should strive to provide those unskilled workers with a proper training to enable them to escape unemployment. Our immigration policy should not be allowed to contradict this manpower retraining policy.
Whether we like it or not, Mr. Chairman, even when reference is made to selective immigration, even when immigrants are required to have certain professional qualifications in order to come to Canada, the fact remains nevertheless that under our sponsorship policy, year after year, approximately 35 per cent of immigrants coming to Canada are unskilled workers. They are being admitted to Canada for a humanitarian reason rather than a professional one.
I feel we should continue to stress professional qualifications so that immigrants come to Canada, not necessarily to enjoy our culture or our bilingualism, but rather to make a better living.
I think that if we accept immigrants, we should see that they are provided with suitable jobs. Otherwise, Mr. Chairman, there is a very serious danger of giving rise to negative reactions on the part of workers. If ever workers realize that immigrants compete with them on the labour market, thus increasing unemployment, then a negative reaction to immigration will take place, and I think nobody wishes that to happen.
That type of immigration should therefore be rational, in that it should take into account our economic situation, our development and growth. But at the same time, it must be humane. And I think that by reconciling those two factors, our immigration policy will really achieve the purposes we are aiming at.


The hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Bell) has touched upon several points and almost insisted that I give a reply to each one of them. I feel he is familiar enough with parliamentary procedure and the ways of government not to expect me to give him, this afternoon, texts that would provide an eventual solution to the problems he has brought up. I can merely tell him, in all sincerity, that the points he brought up do not only interest me, but are of concern to me as they are to the department. We hope to solve them within a short time. Not only that I feel we will have to deal with certain problems even sooner than with the white paper, that is to say we shall be able to solve certain problems before the white paper comes before the house.
There is the problem of sponsorship and that of courts of appeal. I believe those problems can be solved before the overall problem of immigration is looked into.
With regard to the setting up of a court of appeal with wider powers than those it now has, I believe we will come to an agreement; it will be a matter of drawing up a text which is almost ready now and which we hope to be able to submit to the house.
Several members have brought up a question which is of concern to me, and doubtess to others who have not spoken: that of security. It truly is the type of problem one hardly dares bring up because of a persistent feeling that the security of the state is at stake. Only, not talking about it eventually leads to even involuntary abuse of individual rights and freedoms. Sooner or later we may have to re-investigate the whole matter, even if it means taking certain chances.
I therefore fully agree on that point, and I trust the house will approve what recommendations we may make in that respect. For with regard to security, you know, sir, that according to the law certain countries are completely exempted from security tests. The purpose of such security rulings is to protect our country from certain agents. I feel there are times when we are most inadequately protected. Such countries as might be interested in sending spies or saboteurs to Canada would be intelligent enough to send them by way of those countries where there are no security tests. The whole question must be gone into, with due regard to individual rights and freedoms.
I think that any immigration or security system intended not only, and in this respect
June 3, 1966

everybody will agree, to get rid of saboteurs, anarchists, dynamiters and what have you, but also to exert a control on the free and democratic thought of the people, is a bad system. Then freedom is in danger. I think that in Canada, while we cannot afford to be threatened with dynamiting and sabotage, we certainly can run all the risks that involve our freedom.
At any rate, let us say that, with this mentality, we shall move soon, I hope, certain amendments that will take into consideration some of the points raised by the hon. member for Carleton.
The hon. member for Carleton mentioned that one of the objectives as far as the number of immigrants to Canada is concerned could be set at about 1 per cent. Well, 1 think this year, we will get this objective of 1 per cent of the population of Canada and I hope this trend will continue in years to come.
It is a fact that conditions are more favourable this year for massive immigration than they were in previous years. It is more easily acceptable to the people since immigrants can readily find jobs and workers do not have the impression that immigrants come here to compete with them. Now it is a fact that these conditions exist and I think the over-all policy of the department is intended to increase the number of immigrants.
The hon. member for Waterloo South (Mr. Saltsman) spoke about the manpower mobility program. It is sure this program is not perfect and that it will have to be rectified as was already done since its inception in December last. We have reviewed it, we have adopted new regulations, for instance the Bissette case has been dealt with in a special way. We had to work out new regulations in that instance and we shall continue to improve them, so as to put the emphasis on grants rather than on loans for workers who will have to move from one town to another.
I believe we should not delude ourselves on the efficiency of a program aimed at manpower mobility. We cannot move people systematically and massively from Newfoundland to Vancouver or from Winnipeg to Quebec. People are attached to their environment, and I think some ideas conveyed by the hon. member for Waterloo South (Mr. Saltsman) are quite defensible. If we could develop some growth centres in the provinces, this would certainly meet our needs far
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration better and would not require the uprooting of whole populations.
As regards the amendment of the Citizenship Act, in order to ensure equality of rights for all Canadian citizens, there is no doubt that if you are a naturalized Canadian citizen, your rights are more restrictive than those of a Canadian born citizen. I believe that everybody is agreeable to the idea. As stated, everybody has wanted this discrimination to disappear from the act for many years now.
Even the hon. member for Carleton, though well-meaning, did not have time to introduce this amendment. I hope to remain in office long enough to do so, and I expect this will be in the near future, so that all Canadian citizens may be on an equal footing.
[DOT] (5:20 p.m.)
Why not bring it down and we will pass it next week?
Well, unless there is another Spencer case-

We want to get ahead
with it.

Well, I do not think it will be too long. As for the hon. member for York-Humber (Mr. Cowan), he dealt with the Lord Thomson case. Of course, it is a tragic situation, but Lord Thomson lost his Canadian citizenship not because he was decorated by the Queen of England, but because he agreed to become a citizen of the United Kingdom. That is why he lost his Canadian citizenship under a formal provision of the Canadian Citizenship Act. If he wants to get it back, he can easily do it, but the act requires him to come and reside in Canada for at least a certain period of time.
According to the information I have, his case has nothing to do with the fact that he received a decoration; it is rather based on the fact that he has agreed to become a citizen of a foreign country and, as such, has automatically lost his rights to Canadian citizenship.
As for the observations of the hon. member for Megantic (Mr. Langlois) about Canadian workers or labourers who are called-up in the United States, I am ready to discuss this matter with the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Martin), but it does not come actually under my jurisdiction.

Now we will certainly have to try our best, in accordance with the spirit and the letter of the law, to facilitate the access to Canada of people living behind the iron curtain, who now meet with certain difficulties. I think that question was put to me by the hon. member for Edmonton East (Mr. Skoreyko). This is another problem which we have considered. We tried to find out how to put these people on an equal footing with immigrants from other countries, without jeopardizing Canadian security and the proper application of the act.
This is a more involved problem but it is now being considered by the department, and we hope to find a solution which we will submit to you as soon as possible.
Members have dealt with immigrants coming from certain countries of Asia and Africa. All countries are certainly not on the same footing with regard to the Immigration Act. In the matter of sponsorship alone one notices a certain discrimination. Should it be abolished? Personally, I feel that any type of discrimination should be eliminated from every provision of the act, so that people wishing to come to Canada be all on the same footing. Should special cases come up, we could exercise various other means of control. I do not think that discrimination should be embodied in the act itself. Therefore, it is a solution to a problem that we hope to be able to submit to you quite soon.
Now, the hon. member for Edmonton East referred to the case of a Frenchwoman married to a Pole who cannot come to Canada. Her husband is not acceptable here not because he is a communist, but simply because we cannot check his record.
Therefore, this is related to immigration difficulties in the case of those living behind the iron curtain. Those are problems that we will have to solve soon enough and I would even hope to settle them before consideration of the white paper on immigration.
Of course, it gives rise to injustice when it can be said that someone is a communist or a danger for Canada. Very often, when there is a risk involved, we do not impose it upon this country, but rather upon the applicant for entry into Canada. But perhaps it would be necessary to widen the door in this regard so as to avoid certain situations which are absolutely inhuman.
It is the problem that ministers of immigration have had to face in the last few years and I am not alone in this. Besides, I was told

that that was really the place where ministers were buried, because in spite of human problems, we are obliged to apply the law as is. This involves considerable difficulties. If a risk is taken, if at a given time we let a common law criminal or a bandit get through, as it happened in the past, this may result in a general uneasiness in certain quarters.
Anyway, we will seek to adjust the law so that this situation cannot occur again.
Now, we were asked to try and establish a special class for people intending to go into agriculture. It is quite normal to want to attract immigrants to make farmers out of them, but if they farm for two, three, four or five months, and if economic conditions are such that they are attracted to our cities, it serves no purpose.
I think that to accept people with lesser qualifications, ostensibly because they will work in agriculture, is to fool oneself because, as soon as they see they can earn $1 or $2 more per hour in Toronto, these people will leave agriculture. The only way is to bind them by their fare, in other words to promise to pay their fare provided they work on a farm for one, two or three years. But, in my opinion, this is not a very sound procedure in a democracy. I think this is slave labour rather than freedom. Anyway, in such cases, they cannot he forced to stay. I do not believe this is an acceptable method and philosophy as applied to immigration.
The hon. member for Trois-Rivieres (Mr. Mongrain) talked of the balance of cultures in Canada, between the French and the English element. Of course, nowadays immigrants are not like merchandise that one can pick and choose. They must be sought after and we must take them wherever we can, when they are ready to come.
In my opinion, since Quebec has begun to follow Ontario, it should deal with the immigration problem and set up offices in French speaking countries in order to solve those problems. I am sure Quebec will receive full co-operation from the federal government. The Ontario government has been doing this for several years in co-operation with the federal government. This does not create friction of any sort and there is no objection to Quebec doing the same thing, so long, of course, as it respects the law and regulations of the Canadian immigration office. I believe this is the way to preserve this balance rather than at the federal level.

The hon. member for Trois-Rivieres also spoke of construction workers brought into Ottawa. I should like him to give me further information on this subject, because I do not think immigrants have been brought to Ottawa for the construction industry. If there is a particular case, I am willing to discuss it, but I do not know of one.
The hon. member made a suggestion with which I basically disagree when he said we should try to find part-time work for those who draw unemployment insurance.
Unemployment insurance is a type of insurance. The people who get unemployment insurance are not living on public charity. If we give start to competition between workers and those who are on unemployment insurance, I fear we will create an unbearable situation. Those people start working for lower salaries and will finally end up competing with regular workers. To my mind we must instead find regular employment for the people on unemployment insurance, full-time jobs that will afford them a livelihood. We must not allow them to compete against the working class.
The member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow) spoke of a court of appeal-I have already spoken about it-and of the Sedgwick report.
[DOT] (5:30 p.m.)

We have studied the Sedgwick report, but we never suggested that it was our intention to apply or implement it in its present form. Surely there will be some changes made and for the time being I do not think we are in disagreement in this regard.
The hon. member spoke about the report made by Miss Edith Ferguson. All I have to say in this regard is that under federal-provincial training agreements, the decision to establish training programs and extend living allowances is a provincial decision rather than a federal one. At the present time the federal government contributes 75 per cent of training costs and 90 per cent of living allowances for unemployed persons, including immigrants in full-time courses, and 50 per cent of training costs for employed persons taking part-time courses.
The provincial and federal officials will be making arrangements to hold discussions on these matters in the near future. If provincial governments decide for example to set up classes combining language, citizenship and academic subjects for newcomers who need

Although a knowledge of either English or French is not a requirement for admission to Canada, all unsponsored immigrants selected overseas by the Department of Citizenship and Immigration are informed that until they know the language of their community of settlement they cannot expect to realize their full capabilities. Written advice is given to all such immigrants on the necessity of learning either English or French early in the immigration process, and it is suggested to them that they take language instruction prior to their leaving for Canada. This point is further stressed during the interview with the counselling officer, and the facilities for carrying on language instruction after arrival in Canada are explained.
As far as unskilled immigrants are concerned, the department is not selecting such persons abroad unless they meet certain basic educational requirements. We are ready to work with provincial governments in this field, and I hope our efforts in this regard will be fruitful.

The hon. member for Winnipeg North has also mentioned the case of medical doctors who cannot practise even with professional qualifications. In this field, we have already approached the provincial government of Quebec. We are ready to apply again to the Ontario government, if need be, so that provincial governments may bring professional organizations to cease this discrimination, not only in the case of physicians but of all professionals immigrating to Canada. The same thing could probably be asked of our good friends of the trade unions, as they are sometimes a little too conservative in this field. Immigrants must feel at home in Canada and they must be convinced that their professional qualifications are recognized.
But the hon. member for Winnipeg North will understand that this matter does not come directly under our jurisdiction and that we have to leave it to the provincial authorities, which usually control the activities of these private organizations.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to direct a question to the minister. During his remarks I did not hear him say anything about immigration provisions regarding farm workers in western Canada. At one time certain immigrants were expected and required to work on farms for one year before moving to another type of employment. This provision seems to have gone by the boards in the last few years. It is very difficult to get farm labour in western Canada and I believe that some provision should be made which would require certain types of immigrants from other countries to make themselves available for farm work for a certain period of time.
There is no point in requiring immigrant doctors and lawyers who must requalify in this country to spend a certain period of time working as farm labourers. It is much better to have trained farm workers required to put in a certain period of time at this type of work before moving to another occupation. I should like to hear what the minister has to say about this matter. He may well have said something in this regard during his remarks, but if he did I did not hear it.
[DOT] (5:40 p.m.)

Mr. Chairman, perhaps I missed the first part of the hon. member's remarks. Let me assure hon. members that there are a certain number of farmers coming to Canada each year. I do not have the figures with me, but the problem in this regard is that even though these people are required to work on farms they do not stay at that work, for different reasons, some of which are economic. I understand that what the hon. member has in mind is that there should be a clear understanding or even a formal agreement that they will stay on the farms for a while. Is this the question the hon. member put to me?
Yes, Mr. Chairman. If the minister wishes, I can supply him with the names of people who have written to me in the last

The number of people employed on farms in Canada is decreasing all the time and has been decreasing tremendously in the past 10 or 20 years. At the same time, for many reasons farmers have not been in a position to provide competitive working conditions and pay competitive wages. Therefore it is very difficult to counteract this trend. I should like to reserve judgment on this question because there are a number of things of which I am not aware. But personally I am not very enthusiastic about having formal agreements in order to compel a free citizen to stay in a certain job for years if he does not like it, or can find a better job somewhere else. I am not sure that such agreements could be easily implemented or enforced. In any event, Mr. Chairman, I should like to take this question as notice and perhaps I can discuss it with the hon. member. When my estimates come back, as they probably will, for consideration by the committee perhaps I can clarify this point.
Perhaps I would be able to visit the minister in his office and we could talk it over under perhaps better circumstances than these.
The hon. member is welcome to visit me in my office.

Mr. Chairman, I wish to address a question to the minister. Does he intend to make some arrangements concerning the immigrants who cross the border into the United States and who cost a lot of money to Canadians? They do not stay very long in Canada and they go over shortly to the United States. I believe some steps should be taken, and I wish I were informed of the minister's opinion on this matter.

Mr. Chairman, Canada is a country which benefits from immigration. If we consider the final result of immigration, the number of persons entering Canada as compared to the number of those leaving it, we have a positive balance-sheet, that is there are many more immigrants entering Canada than leaving the country.
June 3, 1966

So, if Canada is happy to receive immigrants, I believe it would be quite illogical to try to impose restrictions on people wishing to go elsewhere, because if all countries acted like that, the migration of populations would be impossible.
Concerning the United States, there is no doubt that we incur in deficit on immigration and emigration. In other words, there are more people from Canada going to the United States than there are coming to Canada from the United States. The discrepancy is perhaps of the order of 30,000 people per annum. But on the whole, if we consider the total migration of Canada, we benefit, and if, by any chance, we imposed restrictions on emigration to the United States, well, we should expect the United States and the other countries to do the same thing toward Canada.
This is like people who think they can impose duties on foreign products and that other countries will not. We are not alone in this world.
Therefore if this population migration is to our advantage, we must not be among those who impose restrictions or make a useless fuss. The way for us to keep people in Canada is to create conditions such that they will want to stay. And, between us, if we were to find some advantage in moving to California, because it suits us, or if we had a family and so on, would we accept it if a state made all sorts of trouble for us because we were not leaving? Aside from states and the common interest, there is also the individual. Anyhow, let us say I do not find these restrictions very desirable.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to ask the minister a question about mine labour. I understand that the mining industry is claiming that it is short to the extent of some 6,000 men to fill available jobs, and I know the minister has on several occasions said that one of the reasons for this lack of manpower is the fact that the accommodation and facilities provided in mining towns is not of a quality to keep immigrants to this country working in the mines in these areas.
I should like to ask the minister whether he has had any conversations with the mining industry about means and methods which the industry could use to hold the people that are brought in occasionally, and also to attract Canadians back to these mining areas.

Mr. Chairman, we have met with representatives of the Mining Companies Association to discuss this problem, but we believe that those companies can make an effort in order to train or retrain their staff. They might also strive to improve working conditions so as to attract workers.
At any rate, let us say that we are trying to avoid, by expanding an immigration which might create a problem in Canada at a given time, that some employers be prevented from assuming their responsibilities with regard to our workers and to the Canadian people.
This does not mean that all mining companies seek to have workers for less than they would pay Canadians. Conditions must not be created which would encourage them to adopt this practice.
For instance, a mine was closed down at Bell Island, Newfoundland, where there are close to 1,000 miners in the street. We do not know what will happen, but anyway if there are jobs in Canada, we must give them the preference, we must try and retrain them instead of importing people who are qualified and who eventually will become a burden to the Canadian economy.

Mr. Chairman, I have just one question to ask the minister. In view of the fact that it was only about six weeks ago, or perhaps two months ago, that the minister said it was impossible to run the immigration department under its present policies and set-up-
I said that?

I think it was on March 22. At least, it was reported that the minister said he had lost control over immigration policy and it was impossible to continue on that basis. I wonder how long the minister anticipates it will take, after bringing in the white paper, to introduce the new Immigration Act in the house?
[DOT] (5:50 p.m.)

I think the report the hon. member has given of my statement is a little too broad. I did not say it was impossible to run the immigration and citizenship department; I said it would be impossible to keep control of immigration if we did not solve the problem of non-immigrants in Canada. My statement was not as broad as the hon. member has said. So I think this problem of non-immigrants in Canada will have to be

Supply-Citizenship and Immigration solved before we present the white paper on this subject. I think it will probably be done in a few weeks time, as soon as the agenda of the house allows for it.
My question was whether you anticipate introducing legislation relating to this matter during this session of parliament.

I do not know, any more than any of the other hon. members of this house, exactly what will happen in the next few weeks or few months, but the intention is to introduce this legislation as soon as possible, and probably before the end of June.

I have a question for the minister. I know that in the southeastern part of British Columbia many immigrants come from the United States and receive the status of landed immigrants. However, many of them have no intention of settling in Canada; they come here to take employment at very high wages for a year or two and, as they will tell you, they intend to go back as soon as the job is completed. What will be done to stop that situation? Those people are taking away jobs from Canadians and even from immigrants who, in some cases, wish to stay in this country.

I presume that some
Canadians do exactly the same thing in the United States. Whether you restrict the employment of United States citizens in Canada or the employment of Canadians in the U.S., you have to accept this competition. I think that if we prevent U.S. citizens from coming here and working under those conditions, the U.S.A. will probably retaliate by preventing Canadians from doing the same in the U.S.

Would it not be better, to be quite frank about it, not to call them landed immigrants but to give them visitors' permits allowing them to work here for a year or two? There is a lot of humbug in this now, and I loathe humbug.
I do not know how you can discover the intention of a U.S. citizen who states he wishes to have the status of a landed immigrant and become a Canadian citizen. It is not easy.

Mr. Chairman, I wish to ask the minister a question. Since our western agriculture has reached a stage where it is very technical and where there is a need for people who know something about operating very heavy expensive machinery such as

combines, big tractors and equipment to clear land, would it be possible to allow some of these people to take technical and vocational training in schools which are set up for this purpose at the present time? Our agricultural industry is very complicated at present and it will get more so as time goes on.

I think that farmers can profit by this training allowance bill which is now before the house and which provides for allowances up to $90 a week for training or retraining in primary industry such as agriculture, forestry and so on.
Item agreed to.
